findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — P1, confidence 100 — `Resource resource =  resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()); if (resource == null) { ... resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) }` — Failure mode: the existence of any per-client resource suppresses evaluation of the all-Clients resource, so adding an unrelated object-specific permission (for example `view`) deterministically revokes an otherwise valid type-wide permission (for example `manage`) for that client; instance and type-wide grants are additive dimensions, not an either/or representation.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:86 — P1, confidence 100 — `return canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW);` — Failure mode: a type-wide `manage` grant is omitted from the type-wide view/list decision even though `canView(ClientModel)` makes object-level `manage` transitively view via `canConfigure`, so the same business grant changes meaning by evaluation entry point and a manage-all administrator cannot use list operations unless separately granted `view` or a query role.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — P1, confidence 100 — `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` — Failure mode: client-instance resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` are assigned a name, owner, and scopes but never `Resource.type`, while only the all-Clients sentinel is initialized with type `Clients`; this lookup therefore cannot enumerate UUIDs from specific-client permissions and returns an empty/wrong candidate set to consumers of `getClientsWithPermission`.

server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:83 — P2, confidence 100 — `Resource resource = resourceStore.findById(resourceServer, id); if (resource != null) { return resource; }` — Failure mode: an authorization-resource ID is accepted before the requested `resourceType` is resolved or checked, so a Clients permission can persist a Users resource (and vice versa), creating an illegal cross-type policy/resource graph whose metadata and evaluation semantics disagree.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — P2, confidence 100 — `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) {` — Failure mode: lifecycle cleanup is gated to the legacy feature while the new client resources are owned by `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`; deleting a protected client under V2 leaves its authorization Resource and attached policies dangling, so client churn monotonically accumulates stale derived authorization data.

server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:310 — P2, confidence 100 — `if (USERS.getType().equals(resourceType)) {` — Failure mode: Clients is added to resource creation but not to the resource-name projection, so client-instance resources fall through to `return resource.getDisplayName()` even though creation sets no display name; permission representations/UI lose the client identifier instead of exposing the clientId, unlike the established Users mapping.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — P1, confidence 100: `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) {` is the lone notification gate even though all four evaluator/management selectors at lines 46, 53, 60, and 67 gate on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`; in a V2-only deployment client/role/group removal notifications skip permission cleanup entirely, leaving the deleted object's authorization resources and policies behind.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — P1, confidence 100: `Resource resource =  resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId());` filters by resource-server id, but `AdminPermissionsSchema` creates the same resource with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())`; the owner mismatch makes every client-specific lookup miss and fall back to the all-Clients resource, so the newly added per-client MANAGE/CONFIGURE/VIEW/map-role grants are ignored.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — P1, confidence 100: `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` enumerates typed resources, while the per-client creation path `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` only sets scopes and never sets `resource.setType(...)`; `getClientsWithPermission` therefore omits all per-client grants and can return the type-level resource name `Clients` instead of actual client ids to callers that filter role mappings.

Strongest author rebuttal: the schema is declared in code and `init` already materializes every declared scope/resource; that fails because materialization is only inside the new-client branch, so no code reconciles already-persisted resource servers.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — P1, confidence 100: `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) {` guards client-deletion cleanup with the V1 flag while every V2 evaluator/management dispatch above uses `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`; in a V2-only realm, deleting a client therefore leaves its per-client authorization resource and policies active, and restoring/importing a client with the same supplied ID rebinds those stale grants so a formerly delegated administrator gains unauthorized access to the replacement client. Strongest rebuttal: “the deleted client is no longer reachable” fails because Keycloak realm restore/import preserves client IDs and the orphaned authorization resource is keyed by that same client ID, so the next object with that identity inherits the old policy.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:78 — P2, confidence 100: `if (canView() || canConfigure(client)) { return true; }` returns the all-clients VIEW grant before evaluating the target client's policy, so an explicit negative VIEW permission on a sensitive client never reaches `hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW)` and the delegated administrator can read that client's configuration despite the deny. Trigger: the same subject has a positive all-clients VIEW permission and a negative VIEW permission for one client; consequence: broken object-level authorization exposes the denied client's configuration; affected party: that client and its owner. Strongest rebuttal: “VIEW on all clients necessarily includes this client” fails because FGAP's specific-resource policy is the intended higher-priority carve-out and this short-circuit makes such explicit denies unenforceable.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:149 — P2, confidence 100: `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2");` is executed by cross-client V1 token-exchange audience validation whenever FGAP V2 is selected, converting an authorization decision into an uncaught HTTP 500 and stack-trace log entry; an authenticated requester can repeat cross-client exchange requests to flood logs/consume error-handling resources and the token-exchange service is unavailable for every legitimate cross-client request. Trigger: FGAP V2 plus V1 token exchange with an audience different from the requesting client; consequence: repeatable availability degradation and guaranteed request failure; affected party: the Keycloak operator and token-exchange clients. Strongest rebuttal: “token exchange permissions are unsupported in V2” fails because the deployed V1 exchange path still calls this boolean evaluator under V2; unsupported policy configuration must fail closed with `false`, not throw through the request path.

goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) method in ClientPermissionsV2.java lines 210-235, the logic is: 1) First try to find a resource by client.getId(), 2) If not found, fall back to the type-wide 'all-clients' resource. The problem is when a per-client resource EXISTS (e.g., created for a 'view' permission), the code returns that resource and evaluates permissions ONLY against it, never checking the type-wide resource. This means if someone has type-wide 'manage' permission on all clients, but a specific client has a per-client 'view' permission resource created, the manage permission check will only evaluate against the per-client resource (which may not have 'manage' scope), effectively revoking the type-wide grant. The correct behavior should be additive - check both the specific resource AND the type-wide resource.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in ClientPermissionsV2.java line 86, `canView()` is defined as `return canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW);`. However, `canView(ClientModel client)` at line 76-80 includes `canConfigure(client)` which transitively includes `canManage(client)`. The type-wide `canView()` method does NOT include a check for `hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, creating an inconsistency. A user with type-wide MANAGE permission would pass `canManage()` (line 70-72 shows it checks `hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`), but would NOT pass `canView()` for listing operations since it only checks VIEW permission, not MANAGE. This is inconsistent with the object-level behavior where manage implies view through configure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:149 — P2, confidence 100: `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2");` is executed by cross-client V1 token-exchange audience validation whenever FGAP V2 is selected, converting an authorization decision into an uncaught HTTP 500 and stack-trace log entry; an authenticated requester can repeat cross-client exchange requests to flood logs/consume error-handling resources and the token-exchange service is unavailable for every legitimate cross-client request. Trigger: FGAP V2 plus V1 token exchange with an audience different from the requesting client; consequence: repeatable availability degradation and guaranteed request failure; affected party: the Keycloak operator and token-exchange clients. Strongest rebuttal: “token exchange permissions are unsupported in V2” fails because the deployed V1 exchange path still calls this boolean evaluator under V2; unsupported policy configuration must fail closed with `false`, not throw through the request path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo() throws UnsupportedOperationException at line 149. This method is part of the ClientPermissionEvaluator interface and is called during token exchange validation. When FGAP V2 is enabled, this implementation is used (as shown in MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returning ClientPermissionsV2). If V1 token exchange code path calls canExchangeTo(), it will throw an exception instead of returning a boolean authorization decision. The finding correctly identifies that this converts an authorization check into an HTTP 500 error. The method should return false (deny) rather than throw, as throwing breaks the contract of a boolean authorization evaluator.
